newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Dublin summit to show EU on track, Irish PM says.
newsitem.headline: Dublin summit to show EU on track, Irish PM says.

text.p: Next week's EU summit must show clearly that the bloc is moving forward in all major areas, such as monetary union and the fight against unemployment and drugs, Irish Prime Minister John Bruton said on Thursday.

Bruton, who will host the December 13-14 meeting of EU leaders in Dublin, said he expected progress on economic and monetary union (EMU) and on the fight against unemployment as well as on drugs and organised crime.
In addition, heads of state and government will discuss an Irish draft for a new EU treaty, intended to prepare the 15-nation bloc for eastern enlargement.

"The Dublin summit must give a strong and clear message that we're proceeding forward on all the major agenda items that we have before us as a Union," Bruton told a press conference after meeting European Commission President Jacques Santer.
"I believe that this will give a very strong indication that the Union is on track in the achievement of its objectives."
Santer set out similar ambitious priorities for Dublin.
"If we can succeed in all of this then there will be very clear and strong language coming out of Dublin to public opinion showing that Europe is on the move," he said.

Bruton said there would be agreement in Dublin on the legal framework for the single currency as well as on a new exchange rate mechanism, the ERM2, which will link the single currency with EU currencies which do not join.
In addition, Bruton said he hoped there would be a deal on a stability pact designed to ensure budgetary discipline continues after the start of monetary union on January 1, 1999.
EU finance ministers failed to reach full agreement on the pact at a meeting in Brussels this week but will try again in Dublin on the eve of the summit.
At Monday's meeting, Germany -- virtually alone in arguing for stringent conditions -- appeared to soften its stance slightly, boosting the hopes of a deal.
"We hope that we will be able to finalise that in full at Dublin," Bruton said.
On unemployment, Bruton said he hoped EU leaders would agree on "a very strong statement" noting action taken at Union level to combat unemployment, now at 10.8 percent in the EU.

The Irish paper on a new draft treaty has left out some of the most contentious items such as the right to veto legislation and a "flexibility clause" to allow some countries to integrate faster than others.
Nevertheless, Bruton said it showed that much progress had been made in the inter-governmental conference (IGC).
"We are moving closer together all the time in the positions that each country is adopting," Bruton said.
Santer, saying successful enlargement demanded institutional reform, said the "hour of truth" in the IGC negotiations would arrive during the Dutch EU presidency in the spring of 1997.
The new treaty is due to be agreed at a summit in Amsterdam next summer.
